The Operator is an incredibly immersive first-person game where you step into the shoes of an FDI operator, guiding field agents through tense, high-stakes situations. The game hooks you with its realistic atmosphere, detailed calls, and the way it makes you feel like a vital part of every operation.

At first, you're focused on supporting agents in their day-to-day missions, but as the game progresses, strange and unsettling elements start creeping into your calls. What begins as routine work grows into a gripping, larger-than-life case that pulls you in emotionally and mentally. The story escalates masterfully, and the twists near the end are nothing short of mind-blowing.

While the gameplay is phenomenal, the only downside is its brevity. The main story can be completed in about 3-4 hours, and there isn’t much replay value since the narrative is linear. Personally, I adore this game, but I really wish it had an endless mode with randomized calls or some kind of story expansion to dive deeper into the experience.

That said, The Operator delivers a thrilling, unforgettable ride. For what it is, it’s a masterpiece—and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone looking for a unique and engaging game. Here's hoping the developers expand on this concept in the future!

This game is top notch. As an old school adventure fan this felt like a true Rise of the Dragon, Jeff Tunnell style game which has been sorely lacking in the current market. What I mean by that specifically is that the post-Life is Strange adventure genre has had a long period of hammy, melodramatic social messaging meant to impress small cliques of games journalists for accolades in their astroturfed outlets. The REAL culprit was ABUSE! Or HOMOPHOBIA! Or RACISM! And the game was a METAPHOR! This plot device was not terribly interesting to begin with but due to the applause and funding that comes to such projects, it left us with a decade of such tripe as developers scratched and clawed to be next in line at the Attaboy Club, with each new offering being more hamfisted and alarmist than the last (check my review of 'Jessika' for a hilarious instance of this).

The Operator, however, is just a good old fashioned hard boiled story about cover ups and corruption.  It has a couple of flaws, the primary one being the blurred out bokeh filters meant to act as cutscenes. There is a sorta-kinda in-story explanation for this, and a reason for it to justify a later puzzle, but really it just comes across as a way to avoid paying for cutscenes and as a way to bridge days together, which is understandable enough for a small team with not a lot of money. In future, I'd recommend bridging the days with some kind of interactive option at the character's apartment or neighborhood, or by just using comic book style art for the cutscenes. In any case that complaint is a nothing burger, the game is well worth it and I look forward to more!

So it was a Sunday evening. As it sometimes happens, nothing in my library felt right. So, I went to check my wishlist to see if there was anything that would feel satisfying. I stumbled upon The Operator. And, well, let me tell you, it was everything I needed and even more. I have to say that it's rather short, but just perfect to fill out that one evening of boredom. The gameplay is relaxing for your hands yet somewhat demanding for your brain. I liked solving little puzzles and interconnections. I don't want to spoil anything, but the game gives you huge satisfaction in a few moments when you actually figure stuff out. Wouldn't say it was hard to keep up with all the clues, but I'm pretty sure I still missed some pieces of info. And man, that section when you actually had a timer on, that was really damn cool (no spoilers).

The story? Well, it's great. It kept me invested till the very end, which not every AAA game can do. I have to say that some of the plot twists were quite easy to read, but not all of them. I loved the way they conveyed the story between the work days, never seen anything like it. Sound and music are very important parts of that game, and they were done just perfectly. Nothing else to say here.

To summarize, it is a great experience (that's what I would rather call it) for one evening. If you liked Orwell games or anything else in the genre, you will definitely like this one too. Worth buying, even for full price.

This is a very solid experience. Good X-files story, excellent sound direction and voiceovers. The game does a great job making you feel like you're investigating stuff and not just clicking through dialogue (a problem with many detective games) despite being mostly linear.

The size of it is its biggest weakness, as most reviewers point out. It's not really about how much you get to play, because the game feels well-rounded, there is some good suspense, and there is no abruptness in the story. It's more that the small size of it means that its world, too, is small, and the pool of events and characters in it is small as well. All this makes guesswork easy, so too much of the mystery becomes too apparent too soon.

There is some anachronistic stuff that breaks the spell somewhat, but my time with The Operator has been enjoyable, and I'm looking forward to seeing what the devs create in the future.

The Operator is a really fun, if unbearably short, adventure game that scratches the itch I've had since playing Hypnospace Outlaw. Cyber-sleuthing to solve and aid crimes and slowly diving into a conspiracy? What's not to like?

I wish it was a bit longer or the main plot was a bit drawn out, however. The game starts you off with a simple tutorial, but it drops you immediately into a fullfledged conspiracy that's the driving force of the entire game. Some little bit of fluff would have been nice. Analyze a video to solve an armed robbery, cross-reference tattoos to uncover gang affiliations, find out a victim's next of kin to get more information, or even just zoom in an ID what home a missing cat belongs to. There's endless possibilities for this kind of concept that are just underutilized. It left me wanting more when the reality was I only had a limited set of things to do.

The game is still exceptionally well made and the soundtrack keeps you engaged through all the twists and reveals, even if they were obvious in the first place. It's a good afternoon game.

Tl;Dr: The Operator is an absolute gem and probably one of my favorite gaming experiences this year. It nails its atmosphere and story, with a few small quirks holding it back from perfection.

[h1] What I Loved [/h1]
[h3]The Layout:[/h3] The environments and flow are super well-designed. You’re never lost, but there’s enough to explore to keep things interesting.

[h3]Subtle 90s Vibes:[/h3] The aesthetic is on point—just the right touch of nostalgia without feeling overdone. If you love that slightly grainy, retro tech vibe, you’ll be right at home.

[h3]UI:[/h3] Clean, simple, and fits the tone perfectly. You never feel like you’re fighting the menus, which is always a win.

[h3]Voice Acting:[/h3] Honestly, top-tier. The performances are so natural, and they add so much depth to the story.
Pacing: The game knows when to keep things moving and when to let moments breathe. It’s a tight, well-paced experience.

[h3]The Ending:[/h3] I won’t spoil anything, but wow—it sticks the landing. One of those endings that makes you sit there for a second and just think, wish for more but grow more satisfied with what (little) you know.

[h1]What I Didn’t Love[/h1]

[h3]No Narrative Skip:[/h3] This is a big one for achievement hunters. If you miss something, you’ll have to sit through all the dialogue again, which can get frustrating.

[h3]No Replay Value:[/h3] They’re upfront about this, but I still think it’s a shame. The world and story are so good that even small additions—alternate choices or alternating riddles ([spoiler]Read: Bomb[/spoiler]) or hidden paths—would’ve added a lot.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
If you’re into story-driven games with a great atmosphere, The Operator is 100% worth your time. It’s short, sweet, and delivers an experience that sticks with you. Sure, it’s a one-and-done kind of deal, but honestly, it’s so good while it lasts that I didn’t mind too much.

I understand it's just a game, but this little thing breaks the immersion for me since I kept forgetting throughout the game that I was in the 90s. Also, the game is relatively shorter than I thought it would be. I wasn't expecting 20hrs or anything, but something closer to 9 or 10hrs instead of the average 3 1/2 most people have completed this game. The ending had a great twist I didn't fully see coming, but overall, the ending was a bit unsatisfying. 

Overall, this game I wouldn't consider to be in my top 3 detective games of all time, but I would recommend anybody to play this. Worth a playthrough. The lowest I would give this would be 7/10, and the highest I would go would be an 8/10.
